prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The map shows a store shelf extending across all five frames, generally about 0.5–1.5 m in front of the camera wearer, with the upper shelf edges appearing nearer than the darker floor and recesses beneath the shelves; exact metric distance is uncertain because the map has no calibrated scale. It makes the layered geometry clearer than RGB: products sit behind projecting shelf lips, the floor extends below and in front of the shelving, and some shelf structure continues beyond the top, left, and right image boundaries. Across the sequence, the viewpoint shifts and turns to the right along the shelving, bringing the right-hand display more frontally into view rather than showing an obvious approach to or retreat from a person. No person is reliably visible, so inter-person distances, facing direction, gaze, and human arm reach cannot be established; nearby shelf fronts may be within roughly an arm's reach, but the depth discontinuities and smeared product shapes make fine distances and occlusions unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map marks only a few small regions against black: several product packages are labelled “book,” and one narrow package or shelf feature near the upper part of the third frame is labelled “chair.” Using RGB context, these are almost certainly unreliable class assignments rather than actual books or a chair, although their masks do localize isolated items on the shelves at roughly 0.5–1.5 m from the wearer. The map provides clearer object boundaries and reveals which detected regions are partly clipped or occluded by shelf structure, but it omits nearly all products, shelving, and floor, so it cannot represent the full layout or dependable distances between objects. The detections move from left or central positions toward the right as the camera turns along the display; no people are segmented, so facing, gaze, human reach, and person-to-person geometry are unsupported.
descriptions.pose: The pose map contains two isolated yellow skeleton-like detections, one in the first frame left of centre and one in the fifth frame toward the right, with no magenta hand detections. The RGB frames do not show clear people at those locations, so the detections appear to be false positives on product shapes or shelf contents and cannot reliably establish a person's distance, orientation, gaze, limb position, or reach. If treated only as image coordinates, the first detection is lower and leftward while the last is higher and rightward, but this change is better explained by the moving, right-turning viewpoint and different merchandise than by a tracked person approaching, retreating, or turning. Pose maps would normally expose body orientation and partial limbs despite clutter, but here the sparse, disconnected skeletons, absent hands, and lack of temporal continuity make all human spatial conclusions unreliable.
